reason: The court held this will gave only a life interest, but the statement omits the will-specific wording and surrounding circumstances that made that construction reasonable.
The court held only that the Act did not give absolute title on these facts because no fideicommissum was created, not that the Act never gives absolute title.
The court expressly held that the plaintiff-appellants were entitled to claim the property after Podinona Hamine's death.
The proposition is a case-specific factual conclusion about lot 5 and Kendagahalanda, not a prescriptive-title rule under section 3.
The court considered the defendants separately because their title deeds and prescription claims differed, but the statement drops that condition and wrongly tags Prescription Ordinance section 3.
The statement captures the prescription holding but omits the material requirements of ten years, adverse title independent of co-owners, and the additional circumstances relied on.
The court directly construed section 416 and held that security for costs is discretionary, judicial, reasoned, and reasonable in amount.
The court directly held that section 416 security creates a fund to satisfy costs ordered by court if not paid by the plaintiff.
The quoted holding concerns a section 416 security-for-costs order, while the statement overbroadly refers to making any order.
That section 337 was amended by Act No. 53 of 1980 is accurate but is only statutory background, not the operative holding.
The actual holding was that the original section 337 did not cover decrees for possession of immovable property, which this statement fails to state.
The court made a fact-specific finding that Abeysinghe's title showed no ex facie defect and no contrary evidence, not a general rule that title is valid whenever no defect appears ex facie.
The court faulted the purchasers' notaries for not checking the testamentary position from deeds in their custody, but the statement omits that material factual basis.
The court held that absence of court permission was not an excuse for the purchasers' failure to tender deeds and price, not that it generally does not nullify a sale agreement.
The statement is only statutory background and omits the time limits and statutory preconditions that controlled the acquisition power.
The People's Bank power was accepted as statutory background, but the rule omits the conditions precedent and residence bar central to the decision.
The statement is too vague and omits the actual conditions the Bank had to satisfy before acquisition.
The court held that under the Sisyanu Sisya Paramparawa rule the senior pupil succeeds unless the tutor appoints another pupil in preference.
The court expressly held that an oral appointment requires clear and cogent evidence, and found none on the record.
The court held the documents showed only de facto management and did not establish de jure Viharadhipathiship, which the statement obscures.
The court held the appellants failed to establish excess power in leasing vested land, but it did not construe Land Reform Law section 19 for that rule.
The court held only that serious prima facie questions justified restoring an enjoining order, not a final finding of unfair competition.
The court held that because the Trust was not a legal entity and no valid release occurred, the petitioners remained public officers.
Both the statement and quote are truncated into a vague fragment and do not state the court's procedural holding about concluded Supreme Court matters.
The section 175 bar was part of the holding, but the statement omits the first proviso allowing unlisted witnesses where special circumstances require it in the interests of justice.
